slides.title: Demand shifts before retailers can respond
slides.body: One product connects early customer intent with a decision the business can carry out.
slides.sub: Apparel merchandisers see transactions. They need to see missed demand and act while it still matters.
slides.foot: Plus One Braincell · Team 463980 · Product+ 2026 · Competition concept
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. Open with the case: how can SAP close the gap between a demand shift and a business response?
- Focus on apparel merchandise planners. Sales record completed purchases; missed interest can disappear before the next planning cycle.
- Our answer is one product, SAP Retail Signal, with three connected parts.
- Sources: Product+ 2026 Case Package, pp. 3–5; Launchpad report, pp. 2–4.

slides.title: SAP already supports the retailer’s core business
slides.body: Retail Signal would extend existing transaction, commerce and planning systems with early demand evidence and a shared response workflow.
slides.foot: Customer counts describe SAP’s broader footprint, not the addressable apparel market.
slides.notes:
- 12 seconds. SAP spans finance, procurement, supply chain and customer experience. Existing customers offer an initial route to market.
- These counts are different scopes; they cannot be added together.
- Sources: supplied case, p. 3; https://www.sap.com/engage/future-of-retail.html (accessed 25 Oct 2026).

slides.title: Three gaps delay the same decision
rows: Store teams see what sold, but not which sizes were tried and left behind.
Searching an unavailable size can end without a sale or a restock request.
A price or delivery change needs to be traced to affected products, stores and margins.
slides.foot: Case-based problem hypothesis. Validate the frequency and cost through planner interviews and a pilot.
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. Today’s workflow can involve sales reports, separate website analytics and supplier emails before a planner reconciles stock.
- The case establishes fragmented data and time pressure; it does not quantify the delay. We will measure that baseline.
- Sources: case, p. 4; Launchpad, recommendations 1–3.

slides.title: Meet Bob, before Retail Signal
slides.sub:
Regional merchandise planner
Fictional 100-store apparel retailer
rows: The cream medium top has only 8 units left in Vancouver.
240 try-ons, 43 purchases and 162 out-of-stock sessions are not in his sales report.
The primary supplier needs 21 days; Bob still has to locate transferable stock.
slides.foot: Bob is a fictional persona. Product, supplier and location figures are seeded demo records.
slides.notes:
- 25 seconds. Bob is accountable for availability, but he must reconstruct the situation across teams.
- This is a persona scenario, not a customer interview or measured time study.
- The 80-unit seven-day demand scenario leaves a 72-unit gap after 8 on hand. Low conversion does not establish a fit problem.
- Sources: current Retail Signal prototype; Launchpad report, pp. 3–4.

slides.title: One product, three connected parts
rows: Explain exposure and compare a response.
slides.foot: Working website with seeded records. Joule-inspired explanations and SAP execution are simulated.
slides.notes:
- 90 seconds. Play the recommendation walkthrough on this slide, or open the supplied MP4.
- The video demonstrates all three parts of one product. It uses real captures of our working website.
- Part 1: compare 240 try-ons with 43 purchases, then investigate availability, fit or price instead of guessing the cause.
- Part 2: 162 qualified out-of-stock sessions × assumed 15% conversion, rounded down, gives 24 scenario units for Online West. These are not confirmed orders.
- Part 3: inspect material rates, apply a gas shortage and ask the assistant to explain added costs and margin effects. Then compare immediate stock transfer with later supplier replenishment.
- No live RFID, retailer analytics, SAP tenant or SAP Joule service is connected.

slides.title: Hardware partners and regional delivery
slides.body:
Zebra: fixed RFID readers and antennas
Avery Dennison: garment RFID tags and inlays
slides.foot: Proposed partners, not signed agreements. Availability, product authorization and RF certification require country-level checks.
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. Recommendation 1 needs specialist hardware rather than SAP manufacturing its own readers. Use Zebra readers, Avery Dennison tags and regional distribution.
- Radio-frequency identification, or RFID, identifies tagged garments using radio waves. Room-zone calibration is essential to avoid counting adjacent racks.
- Start with already tagged assortments; tag economics for new assortments are excluded from the base quote and must be priced.
- Capability sources: https://www.zebra.com/us/en/products/rfid/rfid-readers.html ; https://rfid.averydennison.com/en/home/industry-segments/retail/apparel-and-fashion.html ; https://careers.ingrammicro.com/en/locations/ ; https://www.tdsynnex.com/us/en/where-we-are.html ; https://redingtongroup.com/about-us/global-presence/ . All accessed 25 Oct 2026.

slides.title: Meet Bob, with a response he can explain
slides.sub: Seven-day coverage in the transfer scenario
rows: Try-ons, online interest, available inventory and supplier lead time share product and location context.
Compare 40 units at CAD 60 transfer cost
Protect Burnaby’s 36-unit reserve; the nine-day alternative is too late for this seven-day window.
Only goods receipt makes the 40 transferred units sellable in Vancouver.
slides.foot: Simulation: 8 current units + 40 transfer units = 48 of 80 scenario units covered. Sales recovery is unproven.
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. Bob can evaluate a 40-unit transfer at a modeled cost of 60 dollars.
- Coverage rises from 8 of 80 to 48 of 80. Thirty-two units remain uncovered: the tool makes the residual problem visible.
- Approval does not create inventory. Goods issue moves stock into transit; goods receipt adds destination sellable stock.
- Source: prototype seeded transfer scenario, ERT-CRM-M.

slides.title: The first buyers are SAP-connected apparel chains
slides.body:
Primary users: merchandise and inventory planners
Economic buyer: COO / merchandising leader, with CFO approval
First segment: 50–250 stores, online sales and reliable SKU-level stock
slides.foot: Account counts and contract values are planning assumptions, not verified market counts. 150 customers is 30% of the modeled SAM.
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. Total addressable market, TAM, is modeled annual software spend. SAM narrows that to chains we could initially serve. SOM is the share we aim to win; 150 accounts is an ambitious scenario, not a forecast.
- We use a 100-store reference contract. A real account list and willingness-to-pay interviews are needed before funding scale.
- Context: the Launchpad cites US$957B fashion e-commerce in 2026; Shopify corroborates a US$957.31B Statista projection. Consumer sales are not software TAM.
- Source: https://www.shopify.com/uk/enterprise/blog/ecommerce-fashion-industry ; SAP retail footprint source on slide 2.

slides.title: Competitors validate the need; integration decides the fit
table: Use equivalent event inputs in a wider decision workflow.
Connected merchandising, inventory and AI planning
Focus on retailers whose execution already runs on SAP.
Retail planning, scenarios and network intelligence
Bring early intent to a concise SAP approval workflow.
Demand planning and retail transaction context
Extend these products; reuse their planning and data services.
slides.foot: Qualitative positioning from public vendor descriptions. Competitors are commercial offerings; Retail Signal is a prototype.
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. RFID fitting-room insight and AI inventory planning already exist. We are not claiming to invent these categories or to have features competitors lack.
- The case for Retail Signal is a focused experience joining early intent with SAP operational decisions. If an existing SAP deployment already solves the workflow, extend it instead of selling duplicate software.
- Sources: https://www.sensormatic.com/de_de/TrueVUE-Inventory-Intel/TrueVUE-Fitting-Room ; https://www.oracle.com/retail/ ; https://blueyonder.com/solutions/retail-planning ; https://www.sap.com/products/scm/integrated-business-planning.html ; https://www.sap.com/products/crm/customer-activity-repository.html .

slides.title: SAP’s ecosystem can shorten the path to action
rows: S/4HANA holds stock movements and purchasing. Commerce Cloud contributes online context. IBP supports planning.
Authorized product, location, cost and supplier data can make recommendations more relevant to the retailer.
SAP’s large client base creates a potential learning advantage, subject to contracts, consent and evaluation. More data alone does not prove better accuracy.
slides.foot: Proposed architecture. No live SAP integration or cross-customer training is present in this demo.
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. Like an ecosystem of compatible devices, SAP’s appeal is that another tool can work with systems the retailer already uses. This still requires integration work and licensing.
- Our data advantage is business context, not unrestricted access to every customer’s records. Customer data use for AI improvement is governed by service agreements; new development can require additional consent. External model providers do not receive training rights by default.
- Sources: SAP Integration Suite https://www.sap.com/products/technology-platform/integration-suite.html ; SAP responsible AI https://www.sap.com/products/artificial-intelligence/ai-ethics.html ; https://learning.sap.com/courses/building-confidence-in-ai-with-sap/does-ai-train-on-my-data .

slides.title: SWOT: a credible extension with execution risk
quadrants:
Existing SAP workflows
One evidence-to-action experience

Prototype, not production
Hardware and data-quality dependence

Sell into SAP retail relationships
Prove value on unavailable sizes

Strong planning and RFID vendors
Budget pressure and long sales cycles
slides.foot: Strategic assessment by Plus One Braincell; pilot evidence is needed to validate the opportunity.
slides.notes:
- 12 seconds. Our strongest asset is the fit with SAP execution; our weakest point is that commercial value and integrations remain unproven.
- Competition, integration effort and adoption should shape the pilot, not be hidden behind an AI claim.

slides.title: Dependencies come before automation
table: Match SKU / size / location; reconcile stock and timestamps
Tenant sandbox, supported interfaces, roles and audit trail
RFID zone tests; session deduplication; bot filtering
Partner quotes, data agreement and retention policy
slides.foot: Proposed SAP roles: CAR = transaction context; S/4HANA = execution; Commerce = online channel; IBP = planning.
slides.notes:
- 15 seconds. The most important dependency is a common product and location identifier. Without it, the tool may recommend stock the business cannot actually move.
- BTP means Business Technology Platform; Integration Suite connects systems through controlled interfaces, or APIs. A production service needs authentication, monitoring, retry safety and tenant-specific field mapping.
- Sources: SAP Integration Suite, CAR and IBP official product documentation, cited in appendix.

slides.title: Three risks could stop the pilot
table: Confidence thresholds; fresh-stock check; planner approval; reconcile receipts
Stock mismatch >2% or repeated bad transfers
Garment events only; no cameras or identities; aggregate; short retention
Unresolved privacy concern or missing approval
Planner co-design; top exceptions only; matched comparison; capped pilot
No response-time improvement or no path to positive value
slides.foot: Risk owners: retail operations, privacy lead and CFO respectively. Thresholds are proposed pilot gates.
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. These are the three biggest risks: bad decisions from weak data, loss of shopper trust, and a product that does not repay its cost.
- Human approval and transaction reconciliation prevent an explanation from becoming an unverified stock movement.
- Privacy controls require a local legal review; proposed retention is seven days for raw garment events and 90 days for aggregates, subject to that review.

slides.title: Decision rights resolve competing stakeholder needs
table: Fast action without draining another store
Planner proposes; source manager protects reserve.
CFO owns pilot gate and spending limits.
Secure integration and a clear product boundary
Reuse IBP / CAR; IT can block stale or invalid data.
Privacy lead approves collection and retention.
Partners earn hardware and deployment revenue.
slides.foot: Escalation: margin or reserve conflict → retail operations leader; data/privacy failure → pause affected actions.
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. Adoption requires an explicit bargain. Bob gets speed, while the source store keeps a reserve and the CFO keeps spending authority.
- Marketing can promote availability improvements only after results are measured. Procurement validates supplier alternatives; Joule cannot approve a new vendor.
- SAP owns the software roadmap; partners own installation and first-line device support.

slides.title: Trade-offs are deliberate
pairs: Slower than full automation; safer while evidence is uncertain.
Apparel and existing SAP users first
Narrower reach; lower initial workflow and data complexity.
Less coverage; avoids outfitting every store before value is proven.
The demo explains scenarios; live news prediction and autonomous procurement remain future work.
slides.foot: Try-ons and searches indicate interest, not guaranteed purchases or the cause of non-purchase.
slides.notes:
- 15 seconds. We prioritize online demand and shared stock first because they avoid hardware lead time. Then validate RFID in selected stores and introduce supply-cost scenarios.
- Baseline demo rates and material-consumption assumptions are illustrative. Public commodity benchmarks are not the retailer’s contract prices.
- Existing stock does not vanish when new production is constrained.

slides.title: A 12-week pilot earns the right to scale
phases: 5 planner interviews; baseline workflow; privacy and stock mapping.
Online signals and stock read-only; shadow recommendations; hardware zone tests.
10 stores; controlled transfers; RFID evidence; reconcile all receipts.
Matched-store evaluation; cost scenarios; CFO / COO scale or stop gate.
slides.foot: Resources: SAP product lead, 2 integration engineers, full-stack engineer, analyst, UX/change lead; retail and partner counterparts.
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. Start with interviews and a two-week baseline, then shadow mode: calculate recommendations without executing them.
- Hardware qualification can proceed alongside digital integration. If devices are delayed, digital and supply workflows continue; RFID claims wait.
- Scale to a 100-store customer only after week 12. Wider commercial rollout takes additional quarters, separate from pilot completion.

slides.title: Success means a faster, verified response
slides.body: Business gate: positive incremental contribution after transfer costs and returns, with a credible cash payback within 24 months at the negotiated price.
slides.foot: Targets, not achieved results. Compare pilot with matched stores and pre-pilot baseline; report uncertainty.
slides.notes:
- 18 seconds. Measure both median and 90th-percentile response time so an average cannot hide slow exceptions.
- Track signal freshness, recommendation acceptance with reasons, stockout sessions, realized contribution and shopper complaints.
- CFO owns financial verification; analyst owns matched-store measurement; operations owns stock accuracy. If the pilot is underpowered, extend measurement rather than claim causal uplift.

slides.title: One subscription; partners earn the hardware work
slides.sub:
Reference customer: 100 stores
CAD 50k platform + CAD 3k per store
slides.foot: Proposed commercial model; quotes and accounting treatment unconfirmed. Existing tagged merchandise assumed; taxes and new tag programs excluded.
slides.notes:
- 20 seconds. The reference price covers the one product with all three parts. RFID is activated only at equipped stores.
- Of each 8,000-dollar hardware and installation invoice, 5,000 goes to equipment/tag suppliers, 1,000 to distribution and 2,000 to deployment. SAP earns no hardware margin in this model.
- Of 75,000 onboarding, SAP retains 15,000 and the delivery partner receives 60,000. All are assumptions, not negotiated terms.

slides.title: Retailer value must clear the cash-only test
stats: Excludes time unless cash is saved
slides.foot: Illustrative steady-state annual benefits; not measured. Base cash-only payback misses the 24-month scale gate.
slides.notes:
- 25 seconds. Separate productive capacity from cash savings. One percent incremental sales at a 45 percent contribution margin yields 450,000 dollars; time freed is worth 364,000 only if productively redeployed.
- Economic net annual value is 464,000, but cash-only net is 100,000. Upfront 235,000 means 6.1-month economic payback versus 28.2 months cash-only.
- The base model fails our 24-month cash gate. We must prove at least 1.04% uplift, lower price/cost, or documented cash savings before scale. This is why the pilot is needed.

slides.title: SAP’s base scenario reaches CAD 38.1M in year 3
slides.foot: Illustrative, not SAP guidance. Midyear customer wins, no churn, CAD 350k/customer/year; hardware pass-through excluded.
slides.notes:
- 25 seconds. Annual recurring revenue at the end of year 3 is 52.5 million; recognized year-3 revenue is 38.1 million because new customers arrive throughout the year.
- This is a product contribution model before tax, financing, corporate allocations and working capital. Costs include customer acquisition and the proposed pilot in year-one spending.
- Zero churn and 150 wins are optimistic assumptions. Renewal-only break-even is approximately 23 full-year customers at the year-two fixed cost. Sensitivities are in the appendix.

slides.title: Earlier evidence is useful only when teams can act
rows: A prioritized decision with evidence, alternatives and a visible owner.
Better availability and margin discipline, measured against the cost of responding.
A better chance of finding the right size, without personal fitting-room surveillance.
A focused extension of existing retail workflows and recurring software revenue.
slides.foot: One SAP Retail Signal subscription. Shared evidence, shared inventory context and a traceable response.
slides.notes:
- 12 seconds. The value is the shorter gap between a qualified signal and a verified business response.
- Better business context can make Joule more useful, while people retain accountability for consequential actions.

slides.title: A pilot decision, with a clear scale gate
slides.sub:
SAP-funded pilot proposal
12 weeks · 10 stores · one apparel design partner
slides.body:
Approve a capped pilot, name the retail sponsor and agree access to a sandbox.

Scale when response time improves, stock reconciles and cash payback meets the 24-month gate.
slides.foot: Pilot budget included in year-one operating spend. Funding, customer participation and partners remain proposed.
slides.notes:
- 18 seconds. Our ask is a capped 250,000-dollar pilot, a named retailer sponsor and sandbox access.
- The budget covers 80,000 hardware, 80,000 integration, 50,000 product analytics, 20,000 training and 20,000 contingency.
- End with the decision: prove the response workflow and retailer economics before scaling. SAP Retail Signal makes an early signal useful by connecting it to action.
- Total planned main-deck time: 480 seconds including the 90-second video.

slides.title: Financial assumptions and boundaries
table: CAD 75k total; CAD 15k retained by SAP
Matched-store test; net of returns and variable costs
slides.notes:
- All values on this slide are modeling assumptions created for the pitch, not data supplied as actual customer results.
- Prices exclude sales taxes, new item-tag programs and financing. Existing retailer SAP licenses are assumed. Incremental SAP infrastructure and usage costs must be confirmed; if not included in the negotiated subscription they worsen ROI.
slides.foot: SAP Retail Signal · Supporting detail for Q&A · All financial forecasts are illustrative.

slides.title: Retailer calculations: value and payback
table: Annual economic value net of fee
Annual cash-only value net of fee
slides.foot: Simple payback assumes steady-state benefits from day 1; ramp-up lengthens realized payback.
slides.notes:
- First-year economic benefit 814,000; cost 585,000; economic surplus 229,000; first-year ROI = 229,000 / 585,000 = 39.1%.
- Cash-only first-year surplus = 450,000 − 585,000 = −135,000. At the base assumptions, scale should not be approved on economic value alone.
- No discounting, depreciation, tax, inflation or working-capital benefit included.

slides.title: Retailer sensitivity and break-even
slides.body:
Renewal cash break-even: 0.778% sales uplift.
24-month cash payback gate: 1.039% uplift.
First-year cash break-even: 1.300% uplift.
slides.notes:
- Formulas: cash net = sales × uplift × 45% − 350,000. Economic net adds 364,000 capacity value. Upfront is 235,000.
- Cash renewal break-even = 350,000 / (100,000,000 × .45).
- 24-month gate = (350,000 + 235,000/2) / 45,000,000 = 1.0389%.
- Year-one break-even = (350,000 + 235,000) / 45,000,000 = 1.3%.
- At 0.5% uplift, economic payback = 235,000 / 239,000 × 12 = 11.8 months, illustrating why cash and capacity must be separated.
slides.foot: SAP Retail Signal · Supporting detail for Q&A · All financial forecasts are illustrative.

slides.title: Recommendation 1: proposed money flow
slides.foot: Illustrative allocations, not manufacturer prices or signed commercial terms. No hardware revenue booked by SAP.
slides.notes:
- Hardware and installation are customer-funded and separately invoiced by partners in a full rollout.
- The illustrative 12-week pilot is SAP-funded, so the hardware part of that pilot is a SAP program cost instead.
- A new garment tagging program, replacements, local duties, service levels and any channel referral fees require separate pricing. Do not present this allocation as a quote from Zebra or Avery Dennison.

slides.title: SAP revenue and cost formulas
slides.notes:
- Revenue assumes recurring software delivered throughout the year, all wins at a midyear average, and no churn or expansion. Services use net coordination fees, not gross pass-through.
- Commercial principal-versus-agent treatment must be reviewed by finance. This is a simplified product model, not an IFRS revenue-recognition conclusion.
- Fixed costs include staffing, sales, acquisition, operations and the CAD 250k pilot. Hardware margins, tax, corporate allocations and financing are excluded.
slides.foot: SAP Retail Signal · Supporting detail for Q&A · All financial forecasts are illustrative.

slides.title: SAP downside and concentration risk
slides.body:
Renewal-only break-even at CAD 6M fixed spend:
CAD 6M ÷ (CAD 350k × 75%) = 22.9 full-year accounts.
slides.foot: Scenario analysis, not forecasts. Zero churn is optimistic; renewal, sales cycles and cloud usage require validation.
slides.notes:
- Slower wins uses average customers 5, 25, 60 and new accounts 10, 30, 40 with the same 5M / 6M / 8M fixed costs.
- Price-pressure case keeps base adoption but price falls to 300k and COGS rises to 35%.
- Stalled case: ending accounts 20,20,20, average 10,20,20; new20,0,0; contributions −2.075M,−0.75M,−2.75M. Cumulative −5.575M.
- Losses are plausible if sales stall; scale spending should follow evidence.

slides.title: Pilot funding and release gates
table: Capped; included in Year-1 fixed spending
slides.notes:
- The hardware line is a trial budget, not a committed ten-store purchase. Timing depends on device availability and local approvals.
- Customer staff time and existing SAP licenses are contributions assumed outside this SAP program budget. Confirm their costs with the design partner.
- Week-two gate: data and privacy feasibility. Week-five gate: reliable shadow recommendations. Week-eight gate: safe actions. Week-twelve gate: adoption, response time and economics.

Selectable network, editable demo rates, public benchmarks, shortage simulation

table: Shared sales and retail inventory context
Purchasing, stock transport, issue and receipt

Secure interfaces, event routing and monitoring
Explain evidence and call approved business actions
slides.foot: Required products and licenses depend on the retailer’s landscape. Reuse existing planning instead of replacing it.

- Sources: https://www.sap.com/products/crm/customer-activity-repository.html ; https://learning.sap.com/products/s4hana-cloud ; https://www.sap.com/products/crm/commerce-cloud.html ; https://www.sap.com/products/scm/integrated-business-planning.html ; https://www.sap.com/products/technology-platform/integration-suite.html .

slides.title: The transfer demo: conservation of inventory
slides.body:
The proposal reserves 40 available units and preserves Burnaby’s 36-unit reserve.
The scenario covers 48 / 80 = 60%; 32 units remain uncovered.
slides.foot: CAD 60 transfer cost = 40 × CAD 1.50/unit. Two-day transit is an assumption; the 9-day alternative misses the 7-day window.
slides.notes:
- Proposal and approval reserve available stock but do not physically move it. Goods issue records dispatch; goods receipt records arrival.
- Baseline exposure: (80 − 8) × 39 = CAD 2,808 retail value. After feasible receipt: (80 − 48) × 39 = CAD 1,248. This is not realized revenue.
- A 70% lost-sale assumption gives CAD 1,965.60 versus 873.60 estimated foregone sales. Do not present the CAD 1,092 difference as profit or observed sales.

slides.title: Demand calculations and inference limits
table: Conversion is lower; cause still needs investigation.
A quantity to test, not 24 confirmed orders.
Depends on the explicit lost-sale assumption.
slides.body:
Qualify session + SKU pairs; exclude bots and repeated events.
Do not add store and online signals into a unique customer total.
slides.notes:
- Fitting-room counts are aggregated item interactions, not identified customers. POS means point of sale, the checkout system.
- Conversion is purchases divided by interactions. A low ratio may reflect availability, fit, price, merchandising or measurement errors.
- Digital inference should use historical conversion where possible, a range rather than false precision, and bot/agent classification rather than silently treating all machine traffic as worthless.
slides.foot: SAP Retail Signal · Supporting detail for Q&A · All financial forecasts are illustrative.

slides.title: Gas-shortage demo: unit cost and cohort impact
table: 25% less input supply; +30% input price; +7 days; 30-day horizon
329 of 1,309 planned new units; not assumed permanently lost
CAD 15,339.50 on deferred units + CAD 208.22 added cost = CAD 15,547.72
slides.foot: MMBtu = million British thermal units, an energy measure. Production reduction and price increase are independent assumptions.
slides.notes:
- Base cost already includes existing energy; only the uplift is added. Supplier pass-through is how much added supplier cost reaches the retailer, not a retail price increase.
- Weighted margin is calculated from revenue and costs across completed units; do not average SKU percentages unweighted.
- The separate timeline estimates foregone sales using current stock and hypothetical receipts. Do not add that sales estimate to the cohort gross-profit reduction.
- Public benchmark: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PNGASUSUSDM ; benchmark currency/market differs from the illustrative Canadian purchase rate.

table: Specific planner, current workflow, Bob before; pilot baseline

slides.notes:
- Why not just use IBP? Reuse IBP; test whether early intent plus a simpler operational workflow adds incremental value.
- Is the demo AI? The assistant is deterministic; production SAP Joule access and model evaluation remain future work.
- Are these customer results? No. Demo figures are seeded; benefits are modeling assumptions.
- Is the cash ROI good enough? Not yet in the base case. The pilot must prove 1.039% sales uplift or equivalent cost/price improvement to meet 24-month cash payback.
- What about customer data? Authorized within-tenant grounding first; training only within agreed terms and controls.
